The figure summarizes photoelectrochemical (PEC) reforming of waste-derived feedstocks into useful products, and compares several device layouts. Overall, it shows a scheme in which waste materials are first pre-treated into soluble, oxidizable monomers, which are then oxidized at one catalyst while electrons are transferred to a separate reduction catalyst. The oxidation side can generate chemicals, while the reduction side converts water or carbon dioxide into products such as hydrogen or CO2-reduction products under sunlight.

The central idea is a two-compartment PEC cell that spatially separates oxidation and reduction. In these designs, a light-absorbing semiconductor stack drives charge separation: one side acts as a photocathode or photoanode, while the opposite compartment hosts the complementary electrode. An ion-exchange membrane separates the liquid compartments, and labels indicate transport layers, conductive glass, encapsulation, and catalysts.

The figure then contrasts three architectures: a photocathode-driven two-compartment cell, a photoanode-driven two-compartment cell, an integrated “artificial leaf” where light absorber and both catalysts are packaged together with a light-entry window, and a PV–EC system where a separate photovoltaic module powers a conventional electrochemical reactor. Together, the panels emphasize modular ways to couple solar energy with waste oxidation and fuel or chemical production.
